mimosa-hostilis-and-mimosa-tenuiflora-on: Mimosa Hostilis and Mimosa Tenuiflora, One Plant, Two Names
Mimosa hostilis and Mimosa tenuiflora are the same tree. Tenuiflora is the botanical name in current use, hostilis an older synonym the dye trade kept.
dyeing-cotton-and-linen-with-mimosa-host: Dyeing Cotton and Linen With Mimosa Hostilis Root Bark
Cotton and linen take Mimosa hostilis paler than wool. Scour with soda ash, give the cloth a tannin bath, mordant with aluminum acetate or alum, then dye.
scouring-wool-before-a-dye-bath: Scouring Wool Before a Dye Bath, and Why It Matters
Wool carries lanolin, spinning oil and dust, and any of them leaves patchy color. Soak it in hot water with a pH-neutral detergent, without stirring, and rinse.
hard-water-and-natural-dyes: Hard Water and Natural Dyes, What Your Tap Does to Color
Hard water is alkaline and mineral-rich, and it pushes a Mimosa hostilis bath from purple toward brown. Use rainwater, or bring tap water to about pH 5 or 6.
dyeing-wool-with-sassafras-root-bark: Dyeing Wool With Sassafras Root Bark, Step by Step
Sassafras root bark gives warm tan, rose-tan and orange-brown on alum-mordanted wool. Use a pound of bark per pound of wool and hold it just under a simmer.
overdyeing-with-mimosa-hostilis: Overdyeing With Mimosa Hostilis, Purples, Rusts and Greys
Mimosa hostilis gives rose to plum. Over indigo it makes violet and deep purple, over a yellow dye peach, coral and rust, and with iron grey and slate.
